Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient was also directly physically injured; that direct-injury theme is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Threat items center on personal physical danger and hypervigilance in the environment ('back to wall', exaggerated startle), which fits direct personal assault/combat trauma more than trauma to a loved one, and is not well linked to the reported appraisal content.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, this item implies an ongoing need to guard against immediate external danger to oneself. That does not fit well with the rest of the profile, which centers on bereavement-related cognitions (survival guilt, numbness) rather than personal threat exposure. It is also weakly aligned with the formulation, where Threat is linked mainly with Negative Appraisals and not with trigger-driven hyperarousal or ongoing danger monitoring.

The threat items are dominated by nonspecific hyperarousal and reminder reactivity, which usually implies trigger-linked activation, but the formulation specifies Triggers → Threat as inactive. With no trigger content present, 'physical reactions when reminded' is poorly aligned with the stated formulation structure.

'Mistrust: People can't be trusted' is a broad interpersonal appraisal that is not well anchored to trauma to a loved one in the rest of this profile. The other appraisal items center on guilt and emotional deadness, but pervasive mistrust suggests a different trauma pattern and lacks support from the selected threat items.

vignette:
Anh Nguyen was sixty years old, a fisherman who had worked the Pacific waters since he was a boy in Vietnam and later off the coast of Oregon, where he and his younger brother, Bao, had built a modest life as deckhands on a charter boat. The accident happened on a late autumn morning two years ago. A squall came up fast while they were running lines about twelve miles out, and the boat took a wave over the stern. Bao was coiling a rope near the rail when the deck tilted. Anh saw him slip, saw his hands grab for nothing, and then the water swallowed him. Anh dove in after him, but the current was brutal and the visibility near zero. He surfaced once, twice, and then couldn't find Bao again. The Coast Guard recovered Bao's body three days later. The official report said hypothermia and drowning; the weather had been unpredictable but forecasted as manageable. Anh never said it aloud, but he knew the truth: he should have held on tighter, should have made Bao wear a life jacket, should have turned back sooner. That certainty lived in him like a second skeleton.

In the months that followed, Anh did not stop working, but the work itself became a kind of assault. The moment he stepped onto the dock, his chest would tighten and his hands would shake. Certain sounds—the creak of a line, the slap of water against a hull—sent a jolt through him that he could not control. He would feel a rush of heat and then a cold dread, and he would have to sit down or grip something solid to keep from falling. He learned to scan every wave as if it might rise up and take someone else. He stopped going out on rough days, then on any day with a wind over ten knots, and eventually he refused to work past the jetty. His captain grew frustrated, and Anh did not blame him. He had come to believe that no one could be trusted with safety—not the weather service, not the boat owners, not the other men who joked about the sea like it was a pet. He kept his distance from the crew at the fish house, turning away when they asked about Bao, because he was certain that if they knew the full story they would see what he saw: a man who had let his brother die.

At home, he moved through the days mechanically. His wife, Linh, would speak to him and he would hear the words but feel nothing behind them. He had stopped feeling much of anything except a low, constant shame. Sometimes a wave of anger would rise up—at the ocean, at the boat, at himself—and then it would fall away into a hollow numbness that frightened him more. He could not cry. He could not laugh. He lay awake night after night staring at the ceiling, replaying the moment of Bao's hand slipping away, and when sleep finally came it was thin and broken. Linh found him sitting on the edge of the bed at three in the morning, his breath fast, his skin cold. He told her it was nothing, but he was thinking that he should not have come back at all. The guilt sat in his chest like a stone: Bao had a wife and a young daughter, and Anh had nothing to offer them but a dead brother's memory. What kind of man survives when his little brother does not?

He stopped going to family gatherings. He stopped answering the phone when Bao's widow called. He stopped walking past the memorial photo Linh had placed on the shelf. Each avoidance made the world smaller, but it also made the world feel safer—or at least less likely to spring another reminder on him. The consequence was that Linh began to cry in the kitchen, quietly, and then one evening she told him that she could not watch him disappear any longer. She had made an appointment at the community mental health clinic. He went because he was afraid of losing her too, but also because a part of him—a very small, buried part—was tired of feeling dead. He sat in the waiting room with his hands on his knees, trying not to listen to the sound of the rain against the window, because it sounded exactly like the waves that night.
